title: Checkpoint: Myths Around the World
objective: After this level you can compare myths and epics from Scandinavia, India, Africa and the Americas and spot the patterns they share.
summary: Chapter 2's myths were told long before they were written: Snorri explained the Norse myths for a Christian age, and the Popol Vuh was written when Maya beliefs were no longer tolerated.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale: why were so many myths written down so late?
cards.body: Every story in this chapter was told for generations before it reached a page. Here's when each one got there, what pushed two of them onto paper, and the patterns you can now spot across four continents.

cards.headline: Written down as an old world faded
cards.body: Look at why two of these books exist. Snorri's Prose Edda was meant, in part, to give a Christian age an understanding of the myths the old poems alluded to. The Popol Vuh was written when the old Maya beliefs were no longer tolerated by their Christian conquerors, and its author says it is written because it can no longer be seen. Both books caught stories their world was leaving behind.

questions.prompt: Put these myth books in order of when they reached the page, from earliest to latest.
items: The Mahabharata reaches its present form
The Poetic Edda's poems are composed
Snorri Sturluson writes the Prose Edda

questions.explanation: The Mahabharata reached its present form about 400 CE, the Poetic Edda's poems came 800 to 1100, the Prose Edda about 1220, the Popol Vuh 1554 to 1558, and Niane's Sundiata in 1960.
